title: Zero-capacitance bitline: one bonded sense amp per vertical pillar
idea: IFR: 'the bitline has no capacitance, so any stored charge reads.' Backward: in a vertical-bitline 3D array, Cu-Cu hybrid-bond each pillar foot (or each group of 4 pillars via a local mux) at ~300-400 nm pitch to its own sense amplifier on a logic wafer, so the bitline is only the 2-3 um stack height (~0.1 fF) instead of a 1,000-cell planar line.
why: Charge wall (fact 1) and 3D blocker (fact 2): ~10x lower bitline capacitance lets a 0.3-0.5 fF lateral capacitor give today's sense signal, removing the 60-75:1 capacitor etch.

title: Plate-tier capacitor: storage node overlaps an interleaved plate layer
idea: IFR: 'the capacitor takes no extra area or height.' Backward: alternate every channel tier with a thin plate-electrode tier separated by 4-6 nm high-k, so each lateral cell's storage node is a parallel-plate capacitor over its own top and bottom footprint (~0.25 fF at k=40), with no lateral capacitor arm; pair with short local bitlines that need only that much charge.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): removes the lateral capacitor, shortening the cell ~2-3x and lowering the ~26-tier break-even toward ~12 tiers.

title: In-stack binary threshold decoder replaces the 3D staircase
idea: IFR: 'tier selection takes zero area.' Backward: thread 7 vertical select-gate rods through each bitline column and give each tier's series select transistors a binary code of high/low thresholds (set by one coarse i-line implant mask per tier as it is deposited), so a 7-bit voltage pattern on the rods opens only the one tier of 128 whose code matches, an old ROM depletion decoder turned vertical.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and 3D cost (fact 2): deletes the staircase, its contact landings and per-tier wordline drivers, ~10-20% die area at 100+ tiers.

title: Inside-out cell: concentric shells built around one etched hole
idea: IFR: 'one hole builds every tier with no lateral patterning.' Backward: etch one hole through a 100-layer wordline-plane/sacrificial stack, recess each sacrificial layer by a self-limiting digital etch, and fill each annular cavity as nested shells (outer plate, high-k, storage node, oxide-semiconductor channel) so each tier forms a ring cell around the central vertical bitline, gated by its own wordline plane and sized only by film thickness.
why: 3D blocker and litho capital (facts 2, 4): ~1 critical mask per 100 tiers, putting DRAM on the 3D NAND cost curve.

title: Interference-printed array: zero EUV inside the cell field
idea: IFR: 'the array needs no masks at all.' Backward: because the cell field is perfectly periodic, print it with two-beam 193 nm immersion interference (~76 nm pitch) plus spacer quadruple/octuple patterning to ~19/10 nm, with crossed exposures for pillars, and reserve projection or EUV litho for mat edges and periphery only.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): 5-7 EUV array layers drop to ~1-2 total, cutting the ~55% depreciation share of wafer cost by roughly a quarter.

title: Defect-tolerant self-assembled lattice with a learned per-die address map
idea: IFR: 'the array patterns itself and defects do not matter.' Backward: form storage-node pillars by block-copolymer directed self-assembly (hexagonal cylinders at ~12-14 nm pitch guided by coarse DUV prepatterns), accept ~1e-4 dislocation rates, and electrically map each die at test into a compact defect-to-spare translation table in on-die fuses.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): replaces the capacitor-landing EUV layers; remapping makes DSA defect levels, which killed it before, acceptable.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous electrode multiplies capacitor area without height
idea: IFR: 'the capacitor has infinite area in a tiny height.' Backward: deposit the bottom electrode as an alloy (e.g., Ni-Al or Cu-Mn), selectively dissolve the sacrificial metal to leave a 3-5 nm ligament nanoporous sponge, then ALD high-k and a conformal top electrode, giving 4-8x the surface of a smooth pillar.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): 5 fF at ~15-20:1 aspect ratio instead of 60-75:1, cutting the hardest etch and pillar-collapse yield loss.

title: Array-logic-array sandwich: each sense amp reads both bond faces
idea: IFR: 'periphery is free because every sense amp serves twice.' Backward: hybrid-bond array wafers to both the front and the thinned back of one logic wafer; each sense amp takes its true bitline from the top array and its reference bitline from the mirror cell in the bottom array (an open-bitline pair split across the stack), alternating roles per access.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): halves sense amps per bit with matched noise cancellation; ~25% bit-cost cut claimed.

title: Backside bitlines free the front side for capacitors alone
idea: IFR: 'bitlines occupy no space between capacitors.' Backward: build vertical-channel transistors and front-side capacitors, bond to a carrier, thin to the transistor bottoms and form bitlines on the wafer backside (borrowing backside-power-delivery flows), so no bitline contact threads between capacitor pillars.
why: Density and litho (facts 1, 4): 4F2 with relaxed capacitor spacing, ~30-40% lower bitline coupling, and one fewer EUV contact layer.

title: Shield-tier interleave makes row hammer geometrically impossible
idea: IFR: 'no wordline has a neighbor to disturb.' Backward: in a 3D horizontal-cell stack, insert a grounded metal shield tier between active tiers and stagger in-plane adjacent rows into alternating tiers, so every row's nearest neighbors are shields or idle tiers; spend cheap extra tiers to buy isolation.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): >10x lower aggressor coupling removes TRR/RFM refresh overhead (~5-10% bandwidth); the price is tiers, the cheap axis in 3D.

title: Micro-mat activation with sub-wordline drivers built into each tier
idea: IFR: 'an activate opens only the bytes requested.' Backward: tile each 3D tier into 4 kb micro-mats and build an oxide-semiconductor sub-wordline driver inside the tier at each mat edge, so the global wordline only steers a local driver and one ACT energizes 512 bits instead of 8 kB.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~16x less activate energy, taking random reads from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.5-1 pJ per useful bit.

title: Laser-written cube-face bus replaces HBM through-silicon vias
idea: IFR: 'the stack has full bandwidth and no TSVs.' Backward: stack DRAM dies with all I/O routed to one edge, mold the stack, polish that face, and laser-direct-write then electroplate ~2,000 copper lines at 5 um pitch down the cube face to the base die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers TSV keep-out area and TSV-related yield loss, part of HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield penalty.

title: Bank-per-tile memory: DRAM bank footprint equals one compute tile
idea: IFR: 'every operand already sits on top of its ALU.' Backward: lay out a DRAM wafer whose bank grid exactly matches the accelerator's tile grid and face-to-face hybrid-bond it, each bank with a private ~4,000-bond vertical port, so a tile reads only its own bank across ~5 um.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM, a 10-30x cut in memory I/O energy.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM bonded whole to wafer-scale logic
idea: IFR: 'no dicing, no packages, no interposers.' Backward: never dice the DRAM wafer; stitch a redundant mesh across reticle boundaries, disable bad reticles at test, and wafer-to-wafer bond the whole DRAM wafer onto a wafer-scale processor.
why: HBM tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): no base dies, interposers or stack yield loss; ~3-4 TB of memory at <0.5 pJ/bit on one bonded pair.

title: Charge-coupled vertical pillar: bucket-brigade string instead of per-tier wordlines
idea: IFR: 'no tier needs its own decoder.' Backward: make each vertical pillar a 32-stage charge-coupled shift register with three clock-phase gate planes repeated up the stack; bits are clocked down to one regenerating sense amp at the pillar foot and recirculated, like a CCD image column.
why: 3D blocker and periphery (facts 2, 7): three clock planes replace 32 wordline drivers and the staircase; ~16 ns pillar latency at 2 GHz shift, and circulation doubles as refresh.

title: Heterostructure hole-well pillar: capacitorless 4F2 vertical cell
idea: IFR: 'the transistor is its own capacitor.' Backward: grow the vertical channel pillar with a 5 nm Ge-rich SiGe quantum well mid-pillar; holes trapped behind the valence-band offset shift the threshold and are read non-destructively as drain current, written by band-to-band tunneling.
why: Charge wall and destructive read (facts 1, 8): no capacitor at 4F2, gain read, retention set by band offset rather than junction leakage.

title: Contactless e-beam test of each tier before burial
idea: IFR: 'every tier is known-good before it is buried.' Backward: after each monolithic tier, run multi-beam e-beam voltage-contrast inspection to find open or shorted cell strings, and write the defect map into a per-tier repair ROM so later tiers and the controller route around dead strings.
why: 3D yield (fact 2): 0.5% loss per tier compounds to ~40% at 100 tiers; per-tier mapping recovers most of it.

title: Sixteen-tier decks hybrid-bonded with stitched vertical bitlines
idea: IFR: 'unlimited tiers without an unlimited etch.' Backward: build 16-tier decks with modest 30:1 etches, thin each deck to ~3 um, and hybrid-bond decks face-to-back at ~200 nm pitch so each vertical bitline continues through bond pads; six bonds give 96 tiers.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): avoids 100:1+ etches for high tier counts and lets each deck pass known-good test before stacking.

title: Dual-ended mirror pillar stores two bits per 4F2 footprint
idea: IFR: 'two cells in the space of one.' Backward: build a vertical channel pillar with one capacitor on top (front side) and another at its bottom (after backside thinning), split the gate into independent upper and lower half-gates, and tap the shared bitline at the pillar midpoint.
why: Density (fact 4): ~2F2 effective cell without shrinking F, ~1.8x bits per wafer at the same litho.

title: Spalled device-layer stacking: one wafer yields twenty memory tiers
idea: IFR: 'the substrate is consumed zero times.' Backward: after front-end processing, lift off a ~10 um device layer by stressor-induced spalling (or hydrogen-implant splitting), bond it onto the growing stack, re-polish the parent wafer and repeat ~20 times.
why: Scarce resources and capital: ~20x fewer ingots (and Spruce Pine quartz crucibles) per stacked bit; wafer cost amortized over tiers.

title: Cold-side memory: DRAM tiers face the cold plate
idea: IFR: 'memory sits at coolant temperature even on a 1 kW chip.' Backward: flip the 3D stack so DRAM tiers touch the cold plate with logic beneath, and carry logic heat up through dense copper or diamond-like-carbon thermal pillars that pass through dedicated keep-out columns in the array.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention roughly doubles per 10 C; holding DRAM 30-40 C cooler cuts refresh ~8x and makes memory-on-logic stacking viable.

title: Periphery outsourced to US mature-node wafers bonded under array
idea: IFR: 'the DRAM fab only makes array.' Backward: split each die into a pure-array wafer (cells and bitlines only) and a periphery wafer (charge pumps, wordline drivers, I/O) made at a U.S. 28-90 nm foundry, then hybrid-bond them, so the array fab drops all high-voltage and logic steps.
why: Periphery (fact 7), capital (fact 4), U.S. manufacturability: ~40% less leading-edge wafer area per bit, with half the value-add moved into existing U.S. mature fabs.

title: Transistorless crosspoint DRAM with wide-bandgap Schottky selector and capacitor
idea: IFR: 'no access transistor, so cells stack like crosspoint.' Backward: replace the transistor with a two-terminal back-to-back Schottky selector in a wide-bandgap oxide (e.g., Ga2O3 with Pt contacts) targeting ~1e-19 A half-select leakage, in series with a small MIM capacitor, stacked as 1S1C crosspoint decks of only word and bit lines.
why: 4F2 and 3D without lateral transistors (facts 2, 4): ~2 masks per deck and ~4x density at the same F, if the selector's ~1e12 on/off ratio holds.

title: Square-meter memory from idle Gen-10.5 LCD panel fabs
idea: IFR: 'the fab already exists and costs nothing new.' Backward: run 8 stacked tiers of 2T0C oxide-semiconductor gain cells at ~1 um rules on 2.9 x 3.4 m LCD glass panels in under-used display fabs, accepting ~100x lower areal density because processed panel area costs hundreds of dollars per m2 versus tens of thousands for DRAM wafers.
why: Capital and cost per bit (fact 4): ~50-100 GB/m2 at roughly $5-10/GB with no new fab, as a 50-100 ns far-memory tier that offloads DRAM demand.

title: Memory inside the glass-core package substrate beneath the processor
idea: IFR: 'memory takes zero extra package area and sits millimeters from compute.' Backward: deposit several oxide-semiconductor gain-cell tiers directly on the glass core of the package substrate (flat, 400 C tolerant), then build the redistribution layers on top, so the GPU's own substrate becomes a multi-GB memory plane reached through micro-bumps.
why: Data movement and HBM tax (facts 5, 6): removes HBM stacks and interposer; ~1 pJ/bit over <2 mm, with capacity that scales with package size.

title: Anodized aluminum foil grows its own capacitor template
idea: IFR: 'the substrate is the capacitor.' Backward: anodize high-purity aluminum foil into self-ordered porous alumina with 200-500:1 pores at ~50-60 nm pitch, remove the pore-bottom barrier so the remaining aluminum base contacts an ALD TiN plate liner, add high-k and a storage-node fill, and build oxide TFT access transistors on top roll-to-roll.
why: Charge wall and capital (facts 1, 4): capacitor AR >200:1 with no etch tool or lithography on a ~$5/m2 non-chokepoint substrate; cell pitch is ~3x coarser, so multi-level charge must close the density gap.

title: Nanosheet-seeded glass grows high-k oriented perovskite capacitors
idea: IFR: 'k is so high the capacitor can be flat.' Backward: coat alkali-free glass with a Langmuir-Blodgett monolayer of Ca2Nb3O10 nanosheets that template (001)-oriented SrTiO3 or (Ba,Sr)TiO3 growth at <=600 C, giving k~200-300 films that a silicon BEOL cannot host, then stack oxide TFT cells over planar or shallow-trench capacitors.
why: Charge wall (fact 1 needs k~70): ~3-4x that target, so 5 fF fits in a <=10:1 structure and the 60-75:1 etch disappears.

title: Silicon-carbide EV fabs make hot, near-refresh-free trench DRAM
idea: IFR: 'memory never refreshes and runs at 125 C.' Backward: use the 150/200 mm 4H-SiC lines overbuilt for EV inverters to make trench-capacitor 1T1C arrays whose 3.3 eV bandgap gives leakage orders below silicon (hours of retention at 125 C), sold as hot-side memory next to accelerators.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and U.S. manufacturability: refresh energy and bandwidth loss near zero; U.S. SiC capacity (NC, NY) is under-loaded, though first-generation density is ~20-50x below DRAM.

title: Jelly-roll memory: one patterned film rolled into a thousand tiers
idea: IFR: 'a thousand tiers for the price of one.' Backward: pattern one long polyimide ribbon with oxide-TFT memory mats and an edge bus, then wind it like a battery jelly-roll; each turn's exposed edge bus lands on a laser-patterned end-cap whose radius-coded traces act as the vertical interconnect, like battery tabs.
why: 3D tier count and capital (fact 2, 4): tiers come from winding, not deposition or bonding; 1,000 turns of a 10 um film make a 1 cm cylinder.

title: Draw-tower lithography: fiber-drawn coaxial capacitor faceplates
idea: IFR: 'features shrink without a scanner.' Backward: build a centimeter-scale glass preform of low-melting-metal/dielectric/metal coaxial rods, draw it ~1,000x on a fiber tower, bundle and redraw to ~50-100 nm coax, and slice the fused bundle into 20 um plates, each a dense array of 200:1 coaxial capacitors to bond onto a transistor layer.
why: Charge wall and EUV (facts 1, 4): high-AR capacitors with zero etch or litho; the draw ratio replaces optical reduction.

title: Substrate-free van der Waals stack with nanometer-thin memory tiers
idea: IFR: 'each tier is a few molecules thick.' Backward: grow wafer-scale MoS2 channels and hBN dielectrics on reusable sapphire and dry-transfer them tier by tier, so each cell layer (2D channel, hBN, metal gate) is ~5 nm and 100 tiers fit in 0.5 um while the sapphire is reused.
why: 3D tiers and leakage (facts 2, 3): MoS2's ~1.8 eV gap gives very low off-current, and a ~20x thinner tier pitch keeps vertical etches shallow.

title: MLCC-line ferroelectric block: one transistor, many plate-selected capacitors
idea: IFR: 'capacitor layers cost what a commodity chip capacitor costs.' Backward: use multilayer-ceramic-capacitor tape casting and screen printing to co-fire a block of thin doped-BaTiO3 layers where each layer is its own plate line, and bond an oxide-TFT glass lid giving one transistor per vertical column, a 1T-nC ferroelectric chain read by pulsing one plate at a time.
why: Capital (fact 4): runs on lines that make trillions of parts a year with near-zero new capex; low density (~10 Mb/mm2) and ferroelectric endurance must be proven.

title: One-shot epitaxy of stacked GaN electron-gas channel tiers
idea: IFR: 'all tiers grow in one furnace run.' Backward: on sapphire, grow an MOCVD superlattice of 16 AlGaN/GaN heterojunctions, each a 2DEG channel tier with very low off-leakage (3.4 eV gap), then etch gate and storage-node trenches through the stack to form lateral 2DEG gain cells per tier, reusing idle LED/microLED MOCVD fabs.
why: 3D blocker and refresh (facts 2, 3): single-crystal channel tiers with no per-tier deposition or bonding; leakage far below the 13 fA tail.

title: LTPO memory panel: polysilicon sense amps, oxide cells, one glass sheet
idea: IFR: 'periphery and array each get their perfect transistor.' Backward: copy the LTPO OLED backplane flow: laser-crystallized polysilicon (~100 cm2/Vs) on glass for sense amps, decoders and I/O, with low-leakage IGZO 2T gain cells stacked above, so one glass die holds fast periphery and long-retention cells.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and capital: periphery-under-array on the same sheet in existing display LTPO lines; seconds of retention cut refresh ~100x.

title: Paper-stack tiers laminated with z-axis anisotropic conductive film
idea: IFR: 'stacking tiers is as easy as stacking paper.' Backward: build each memory tier on a reusable glass carrier over a laser-release layer, peel it off as a 5 um polyimide film, and laminate dozens of films with anisotropic conductive film whose particle chains conduct only vertically through aligned pads.
why: 3D tiers and HBM tax (facts 2, 6): known-good films are tested before lamination; no TSVs or hybrid-bond tools, and carriers are reused.

title: Remote-epitaxy peel-and-stack single-crystal oxide channel films
idea: IFR: 'every tier has a single-crystal channel and the substrate lasts forever.' Backward: grow single-crystal beta-Ga2O3 or In2O3 channel films by remote epitaxy through a graphene layer on a reusable seed crystal, exfoliate each film, and transfer it as the channel of each 3D tier.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): single-crystal ultra-wide-gap channels remove the grain-boundary leakage tail of deposited oxides; seed reuse removes substrate cost.

title: Ion-track membranes: particle-drilled pores averaged into capacitor cells
idea: IFR: 'pores drilled by particles, with no lithography.' Backward: irradiate a polyimide or glass sheet with swift heavy ions (~1e10-1e11 tracks/cm2), etch the latent tracks into ~20 nm pores 1-2 um deep, ALD-coat electrode/high-k/electrode, and bond a periodic TFT pad grid on top so each pad collects ~10 random pores whose capacitance averages statistically.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): tens of fF per cell with no etch tool, enough for 2-3 bits per cell; randomness is handled by averaging, not alignment.

title: Femtosecond-laser-written volumetric memory inside a glass block
idea: IFR: 'the array is written in the volume with no layers at all.' Backward: focus femtosecond pulses inside a doped glass block to precipitate conductive nanowire lines, laser-crystallized high-k capacitor voxels and oxide-semiconductor channel segments, writing word lines, bit lines and cells in 3D at ~0.5-1 um voxel pitch in one machine.
why: Capital (fact 4): a ~$1M laser writer instead of a fab; ~1e9 cells per mm3 if laser-formed devices switch reliably.

title: Carbon-nanotube CMOS periphery on glass beneath oxide arrays
idea: IFR: 'periphery is fast, complementary and made at 200 C.' Backward: deposit aligned >99.99% semiconducting carbon-nanotube films on glass, build n- and p-type CNFET sense amps and decoders at <=250 C, then stack oxide-semiconductor cell tiers directly above with no thermal damage.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and 3D: complementary periphery-under-array with no silicon wafer, enabling unlimited monolithic tiers above; ~3-10x lower logic energy than oxide-only periphery.

title: Substrate-agnostic memory credit to convert existing non-silicon fabs
idea: IFR: 'new memory capacity appears in months, not 3-5 years.' Backward: extend the 48D advanced-manufacturing credit plus DoD/DOE guaranteed-offtake contracts to memory made on glass, foil or SiC substrates, and fund conversion kits (oxide ALD, panel steppers) for existing U.S. display, thin-film-PV and power-semiconductor lines.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4): uses already-built non-silicon fabs; conversion at ~5-10% of a DRAM fab's cost per unit of capacity.

title: Stamped capacitors: nanoimprinted pillar forest on glass panels
idea: IFR: 'capacitors are stamped like coins, not etched.' Backward: UV-nanoimprint a hexagonal forest of 20:1 resin pillars onto a glass panel from a reusable master, ALD-coat them with electrode/high-k/electrode, optionally burn out the resin core for a double-sided shell, and build oxide TFTs above.
why: Litho and etch capital, charge wall (facts 1, 4): one stamp replaces EUV litho plus a 60:1 dry etch; masters are reused ~10,000 times.

title: Fluidic self-assembled memory-tile carpet on a glass panel
idea: IFR: 'memory chips place themselves.' Backward: make 100 um oxide-on-glass memory tiles with shape-coded keys and solder-coded faces, pour them as a slurry over a glass panel with matching wells, and let capillary and solder self-alignment seat millions in minutes, then wire them with panel redistribution layers.
why: Packaging and HBM tax (fact 6): tiny known-good tiles give ~99% effective yield; ~1e6 tiles/hour assembly without pick-and-place.

title: Spatial-ALD roll-to-roll steel foil deposits 64-tier stacks
idea: IFR: 'tiers deposit at newspaper speed.' Backward: run stainless-steel foil past spatial-ALD heads (precursor zones split by gas curtains, no pump-down cycles) to lay a 64-tier channel/dielectric superlattice continuously at meters per minute, then pattern vertical holes by roll nanoimprint and fill.
why: Capital (fact 4) and 3D deposition cost: ~10x lower deposition tool cost per tier than batch vacuum ALD/CVD on a cheap U.S.-available foil.

title: Coolant-in-substrate microchannel glass keeps stacked memory tiers cold
idea: IFR: 'heat never reaches the memory.' Backward: fuse two glass sheets with etched microfluidic channels into the substrate itself, build oxide memory tiers directly on top, and pump coolant 50 um below the cells so memory placed under a hot accelerator stays near 30 C.
why: Refresh and data movement (facts 3, 5): memory can sit directly beneath compute; leakage halves every ~10 C, cutting refresh ~8x.

title: See-through substrate: backside flood exposure self-aligns every tier
idea: IFR: 'every tier aligns perfectly with no extra masks.' Backward: because glass is transparent, pattern the opaque wordline grid once, then expose each later tier's photoresist with UV flood light from the back of the panel, using the buried metal as an automatic mask so every tier's features self-align with zero overlay error.
why: Litho capital (fact 4) and 3D overlay: masks per tier fall toward zero and the overlay budget vanishes, allowing tighter pitches on cheap panel steppers.

title: Light-through-glass optical buses replace vias between stacked dies
idea: IFR: 'tiers talk with no wire between them.' Backward: in a stack of thin transparent glass memory dies, put transfer-printed micro-LED emitters and oxide photodiodes in aligned columns with metal-free windows, so each die sends and receives its data bus optically straight through the dies above and below.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSVs or bonds in the data path and dies are swappable; ~0.5 pJ/bit at 1-10 Gb/s per channel, thousands of channels per die.
